title: Exeter UFO Festival 2026: Your complete guide to out-of-this-world speakers and events
excerpt: Exeter is gearing up for a weekend of UFO lore, costumes, speakers and out‑of‑this‑world fun.
content:
Aug. 31, 2026, 5:01 a.m. ET

  • The Exeter UFO Festival is a Labor Day weekend tradition celebrating the 1965 "Incident at Exeter."
  • Hosted by the Exeter-Area Kiwanis Club, the two-day event features UFO expert talks, a parade, and an alien costume contest.
  • Activities include trolley rides to the 1965 sighting location and continuous showings of historical videos.
  • Proceeds from the festival and a special police patch sale support local children's charities and scholarships.

If you’ve walked through downtown Exeter lately, you may have spotted neon‑green alien faces peering from storefronts and posters — a sure sign that the UFO Festival is about to return.

The Labor Day weekend tradition celebrates the famed 1965 “Incident at Exeter,” when a mysterious red light startled locals and became one of the most well-documented UFO sightings in history.

Hosted by the Exeter‑Area Kiwanis Club, the two‑day festival draws thousands and features talks by UFO specialists, an alien costume and pet contest, a parade, trolley rides, and plenty of food and souvenirs. New this year is a belly‑dancing performance, with dancers staying afterward to teach kids how to hula hoop. Activities will run throughout the town center from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

“It’s growing exponentially each year," said Connie Cox, a member of the Exeter Area Kiwanis.

The story behind Exeter’s most famous close encounter

The festival traces back to the early morning hours of Sept. 3, 1965, when Exeter police began receiving calls about flying objects following people. One woman even reported being chased by a red‑lit craft while driving on Route 101.

Two hours later, Norman Muscarello, an 18-year-old Navy recruit, reported seeing a strange light in the woods near Kensington as he hitchhiked home from nearby Amesbury, Massachusetts. 

Two police officers and Muscarello later returned to the area where Muscarello said he saw the object over a Kensington farmhouse. The officers reported they also saw a flying object they couldn’t explain.

Highly publicized, according to a newspaper account, the men described the object as “about the size of a house,” adding that it “hovered silently over the nearby farm buildings, frightening animals in the barn before disappearing in the distance.”

Although the sighting took place in Kensington, it was famously attributed to Exeter in John Fuller’s book “Incident at Exeter.”

According to news reports, U.S. Air Force representatives said the sightings might be traced to one of five B-47 bomber aircraft flying in the area at that time, or perhaps it could be a mirage caused by a temperature inversion. At the time and since 1956 during the height of the Cold War, the current Pease Tradeport was the former Pease Air Force Base, a hub of the nation’s Strategic Air Command, where B-47 nuclear bombers were stationed.'

One of the festival’s signature attractions is the trolley ride to the Kensington location of Muscarello’s 1965 sighting. The narrated rides run both days from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., with $5 tickets sold at the Trolley Station at 10 Front Street.

Also, historic videos regarding the "Incident at Exeter" will be shown continuously on the second floor of the Town Hall from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and are about 10 minutes long.

Experts to talk on all things aliens and UFOs

The two-day festival features 10 speakers kicking off Saturday, Sept. 5, at 9 a.m. at the Exeter Town Hall with Valerie Lofaso, who will give a talk titled “Using Meditation to Connect with ETs.”

Her talk explores the practice of human‑initiated contact with non‑human intelligences through focused intention, meditation, and coherent consciousness. Lofaso will also discuss the search for extraterrestrial life amid growing interest in UFOs and UAPs, and outline ways people can actively pursue what she describes as “conscious contact.”

Also on Saturday, Ralph Blumenthal will present “Lilac Eyes: Brazil’s Alien Mystery — The 1996 Varginha Case” at 10:30 a.m. Roswell researcher Tom Carey follows at noon with a talk on deathbed confessions, and at 2 p.m. Kathleen Marden — the niece of Betty and Barney Hill — will deliver “The Betty and Barney Hill UFO Abduction 65th Anniversary Presentation,” revisiting the first U.S. abduction case to undergo scientific investigation.

Tim Binnall will close out the day at 3:30 p.m. with “Did You See That?! — UFO Sightings on Classic Sitcoms.”

Sunday’s lineup on Sept. 6 features Laird Scranton at 9:15 a.m. with “Ancient Tutorial on Plasma Energetics,” followed by Martin Willis at 10:45 a.m. presenting “From Flying Saucers to UAP: The U.S. Government’s Response Since 1947.” At 1 p.m., Jimmy “Mr. Haunted” Petonito will deliver “Journey into Ghosts, UFOs, Cryptids and Urban Legends,” and Peter Robbins will close the day at 2:30 p.m. with “UFO Revelations and the Individual: A Fast Ride Through My Fifty Years in Ufology.”

Tickets for both days of talks can be purchased for $40. Speakers will also be selling their books at the events. 

UFO enthusiasts who want to meet the speakers up close can come to a Meet and Greet with them on Saturday at Otto’s Restaurant at 5:30 p.m. The cost is $20. 

When is the Alien Costume & Alien Pet Contest?

Have the perfect outfit for your dog, cat, or child? The Alien Costume Contest and Alien Pet Contest return at noon on Saturday. Kids ages 12 and under are invited to show their alien flair and march in a parade forming on the sidewalk next to the town hall common and heading to the bandstand. Pets, meanwhile, can strut their intergalactic style at the town hall common — the more out‑of‑this‑world the costume, the better.

Food, kid activities and UFO Festival swag

For the first time, local belly dancers will perform at 10 a.m. on the town hall common park and will stay to teach kids to use hula hoops. 

Cox described it as a “unique and different” addition to the festival’s many events for both people interested in ufology and families looking for activities to do with children. 

The Exeter Area Kiwanis Club will provide food and refreshments at the tent by the Gazebo. Expect carnival-type food and drinks such as hot dogs, hamburgers, potato chips and sodas to be served from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The UFO Festival Souvenir Shop will run from 8:30 a.m. until 5 p.m., outside Exeter Town Hall, featuring T-shirts, mugs, tote bags, caps, posters and more. 

The same merchandise sold at the UFO Festival is also available at Trends at 85 Water Street.

Kids' activities such as lawn games, face painting, "UFO Crash Site" creations, gifts, and free refreshments will take place at Town Hall Common.

Get your Exeter police 'Incident at Exeter' patch

For the fifth year, festival‑goers can purchase the Exeter Police Department’s special “Incident at Exeter” patch, with proceeds supporting the department’s comfort dog, Maple. Officers will be at the Exeter Bandstand beginning at 8:30 a.m. on Sept. 5 to sell the 2026 patch for $10.

This year’s winning design — created by a student at Lincoln Street School — features Maple, a farmer, a cow, and an alien in a UFO.

Only 500 patches are available, and once they’re gone, they’re gone. Every dollar raised helps cover Maple’s food, veterinary care, and the supplies she needs to continue her work in the community.

UFO Festival proceeds support the Exeter community

The Exeter-Area Kiwanis Club is a small group of 12 people who put on this festival every year, and Cox encourages people to join or volunteer to help with the festival by reaching out to her at 603-770-8117.

“We need volunteers if there’s anyone out there who wants to help,” she said. 

Every dollar raised at the festival goes back to local children, from building Planet Playground and providing free bike helmets to donating $2,000 in Christmas gifts. The Kiwanis Club also gives out $12,000 in scholarships each year, shared between Exeter High School and the Seacoast School of Technology.

“The Kiwanis would love people to come because this is our largest fundraiser and all the proceeds for this local fundraiser go to local children,” Cox said.
